summary: Proposes an Interagency Research Internet as the natural outgrowth of the current Internet. It is an idea paper meant to start discussion about how to plan and implement it.

eli5.summary: A group of agencies had many separate networks. This memo suggests joining them into one shared research network and asks everyone what they think.

questions: what was the interagency research internet
how was the research internet planned
what role did tcp ip play in interconnecting networks
subtitle: A blueprint for connecting federal research networks into a unified internet.

tldr.problem: Federal agencies each operate separate research networks, leading to duplication and inefficiency. Scientists need seamless access to resources across agency boundaries.
tldr.mechanism: The Interagency Research Internet (IRI) proposes a federated structure where agencies keep their own networks but interconnect them using TCP/IP gateways, shared management, and coordinated research.
tldr.outcome: This plan laid the groundwork for how federal research networks would coordinate, though the specific IRI organization was superseded by other developments in Internet governance.

facts.label: Phases
facts.value: Two: Functional Interoperability, then Full Capability

today: RFC 1015 is a historical record of 1987 planning. The specific IRI organization proposed was not adopted, but the concepts—federal agencies coordinating on research networks using TCP/IP gateways and shared governance—shaped the actual evolution of NSFnet and the national research internet infrastructure.

sections.title: Building One Network from Many
sections.content:
By 1987, the scientific community had spread across several federal networks—Arpanet, MFEnet, NSFnet, and others—each supported by a different agency. While researchers needed to access supercomputers, databases, and colleagues across all these networks, the informal interconnections were inefficient and fragmented.

The RFC proposes the Interagency Research Internet (IRI): a coordinated effort where participating agencies (initially DARPA, NSF, DOE, and NASA) agree to interconnect their networks using a common protocol (TCP/IP) and shared infrastructure, while each agency retains control of its own network.
sections.eli5: Instead of each agency running its own separate network, they decide to plug their networks together and share the cost of the connecting hardware.

sections.title: Why Interconnection Matters
sections.content:
The RFC identifies four key reasons for a unified research internet. First, it avoids wasteful duplication: when a scientist at a university is funded by multiple agencies, the university should not need separate connections to each agency network. Second, interconnection enables cross-disciplinary research by allowing scientists supported by different agencies to collaborate without regard to funding source.

Third, a coordinated research and development program across agencies allows shared investment in evolving networking technology, rather than each agency working in isolation. Fourth, interconnection permits efficient use of existing resources—a scientist should be able to reach supercomputers and databases across the entire interconnected system.
sections.eli5: When networks are separate, it is wasteful and hard for scientists to work together. Plugging them together saves money and makes research easier.

sections.title: How TCP/IP Interconnection Works
sections.content:
The RFC explains the Internet model: special computers called gateways (or routers) are installed at the boundaries between networks. These gateways use the Internet Protocol (IP) to route data packets between networks, and TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) ensures reliable, ordered delivery.

With gateways in place, any computer on any agency network can address any other computer uniformly, even though the underlying networks may use different technologies. The combination of IP for routing, TCP for reliability, and domain naming makes this a practical solution that was already proven on the existing Arpanet.
sections.eli5: Gateways are like post offices at the border between networks—they know how to forward a package from one network to another, even if the two networks work differently inside.

sections.title: Running the Shared Infrastructure
sections.content:
The RFC proposes a governance structure: a Policy Board of agency representatives sets direction, advised by a Technical Advisory Board of engineers and researchers. A non-profit organization called the Interagency Research Internet Organization (IRIO) would be contracted to operate the gateways and provide user support services.

Importantly, the IRIO does not manage individual agency networks; it manages only the interconnections and shared services. Each agency retains full control and responsibility for its own network. This federal-style approach allows cooperation without loss of agency authority.
sections.eli5: An independent organization is hired to run the connecting hardware and help scientists use the network, while each agency still runs its own network the way it wants.

sections.title: Phased Rollout and Funding
sections.content:
The plan proposes a two-phase approach. Phase I establishes functional interoperability: gateways are installed, an operations center is set up, and basic user services (like a white pages directory) are provided. Phase II adds enhanced capabilities: higher-performance gateways, support for international standards, and possible shared backbone networks for high-bandwidth traffic.

The estimated budget for Phase I was about $10 million per year in capital and operations costs, shared equally among participating agencies. Agencies would also fund ongoing research coordination through the Internet Research Activities Board (IRAB) to develop new networking technologies.
sections.eli5: The first stage gets the basic connections working and provides help to scientists. The second stage adds faster equipment and new capabilities.
